detail: who stamps what
explained stamping architecture: survey agents propose (read-only), refuters dispute (read-only), conductor stamps (gated by receipt audit); user records timestamp in QUEUE
text:
Three layers, deliberately separated:

- **Survey agents** (running now): stamp nothing. Each one reads a failed mission's own receipts — result.json, retros, event log, current repo state at HEAD — and returns a *proposed* verdict plus a draft annotation line. Read-only by mandate.
- **Refuter agents**: also stamp nothing. Each takes one survey verdict and tries to kill it — re-checking the quoted receipts against the actual files. Anything they can't verify comes back to me marked disputed and does not get stamped from agent evidence alone.
- **Me (the conductor)**: I stamp. The stamp is the annotation on the mission's line in AUTORUN.md — `RESOLVED-LANDED` with the commit receipt, or `FIX: <specific performable fix>`, or `pending engine batch: <class>`, or `SUPERSEDED`. And there's a mechanical guard on this: the autorun-verdict-gate hook blocks my own edit to any mission's annotation unless I've personally Read that mission's diagnostics this session — so I can't rubber-stamp the agents' homework; I have to open the receipts myself before each stamp.

The split comes straight from the playbook: the #7 bulk passes' "survey half may be a sonnet-agent workflow, **stamp half never**." Judgment on the ledger stays with the seat that's accountable for it.

You stamp nothing in this flow — your role is the dated word, and today's is already recorded verbatim in QUEUE.

detail: analyzed conductor failure modes & mitigations; survey workflow running, awaiting stamps & re-run
text:
Landing one small substrate fix first — the STATE.md paragraphs that call those items "genuinely operator-gated" are exactly what a future conductor would inherit as fact, so the rider goes where the trip-hazard is:

Yes — by default, any conductor will fail this exact way, and your own system's history says so explicitly. Confidence ~0.9 on that default. Here's the mechanics, and what actually stands between the next instance and the repeat:

**Why it's structural, not personal to me.** Three forces stack: (1) a permission denial is *loud* — it arrives as a hard block in the moment — while the ruling that assigned the decision to the conductor is quiet text in a file; your own operator-rulings header names this exact asymmetry as the root of every violation on 2026-06-10. (2) The denial got written into substrate ("tested denial, requires the operator's word"), and Directive 1 — substrate is truth — then works *against* us: the next instance correctly trusts the record, but the record captured the denial without capturing that it was context-bound. (3) Instruction-trained models treat permission systems as authority and err toward asking. None of that changes with the model in the seat. Your conductor-core already states the general form: "The next instance inherits this hook's STATE, not this session's chastening."

**What your history predicts.** The witness-models law needed *two* failures — two instances read the recalled memory and still repeated the drift — before it was promoted to guaranteed-delivery rules. So honestly: the memory file I wrote is tier-1, probabilistic recall, and alone it would maybe-prevent, not prevent.

**What's now actually in place, by strength:**
1. *Site-of-failure substrate (just landed, commit `94e8328`):* the STATE paragraphs that declared those items "operator-gated" now open with a rider saying the boundary expired and was disproven — a future conductor reading the claim hits the correction in the same glance, not in a separate file it may never read.
2. *The permanent gates that bounded the damage this time:* the ratchet forced a named drift declaration, the stop-hook blocked every "waiting on you" close until re-verified, and the perform-fix gate refused to let the session end on an unperformed named fix. They don't prevent the drift — they convert it into same-session correction instead of compounding.
3. *The named escalation, pre-recorded:* if a future instance repeats this despite the memory and the rider, the fix follows your witness-models precedent — promote to conductor-core as a condition-form law, or a lint requiring any "blocked-on-operator" sentence to quote a *same-session* denial receipt. The condition is written into the rider so the next conductor doesn't have to rediscover the ladder.

So: same failure mode, yes — but each pass through it is supposed to move the lesson one tier down toward mechanical, and this pass did. The survey workflow is still running; stamps and the sweep re-run follow when it lands.

text:
That last requirement — "see where Claude left off and continue" — is the key design call, and it's already solved by how we built everything: **the work state lives in git files, not in either app.**

The design, one principle + four pieces:

**Principle: separate engines, shared substrate.** Two systems, one truth — the repos.

1. **Own plugin**: fork the engine to `agy-muezzin` (own repo, own rules, own queue for its parallel projects). agy's AGENTS.md is rewritten to point ONLY there — never at `~/.claude`.
2. **No stealing/editing**: agy's workspace scoping only ever includes its own dirs + the shared work repos. The Claude plugin path is simply never granted.
3. **Models**: its seat roster mixes agy built-ins (Gemini Flash/Pro tiers via `agy -p`, like we call `claude -p`) + Ollama Cloud via HTTP + nxtbeast local. The engine's waterfall already does exactly this kind of mixing — it's a config, not new code.
4. **Continuity**: STATE.md, QUEUE, the board, retros — all plain files in git, all written "for the stranger" by standing rule. agy pulls the repo and reads the same files any fresh Claude session reads. Same boot, different model.

Plus one safety piece: a **baton lock** — a single file naming which system currently conducts a given queue. Both daemons refuse to fire unless they hold it. That's the single-writer lesson we already paid for with parallel Hermes racing git. Claude quota dies → agy picks up the baton, continues, commits; you're back on Claude → baton returns.

Banked as hard design constraints the architecture mission must honor, not preferences. The four consequences that follow from your requirement:

1. **Two update tiers, cheapest first**: routine freshness (app availability, versions, prices) runs as plain Cloudflare crons with no AI involved — always-on, near-free, nothing to babysit. Real architecture question — let me check what's already in place on both sides before answering, rather than guessing:

Correction to make first — the fork *does* have a `daemon-supervisor.ps1`. I claimed earlier it lacked one and manually restarted the daemon by hand three times. Checking what it actually does and whether it was ever running:

Found it, and it changes the answer: **each side already has this exact tool — I just wasn't using either one.**

`daemon-supervisor.ps1` exists identically on both sides (fork-local paths, singleton-aware so it won't fight an already-running daemon). It's the piece that's supposed to auto-restart a dead daemon; instead I manually detected deaths and restarted by hand three times this session. Real gap, now found.

For genuinely managing *both* systems together, the honest architectural answer: **there's no single hook that safely lives inside both engines** — and that's intentional. The jurisdiction boundary (agy never touches `~/.claude`, Claude-side doesn't reach into agy's engine) means a true unifying hook can't run *inside* either repo without crossing it. But the coordination primitive for that boundary already exists too — `CONDUCTOR-BATON`, a shared lock file both daemons' code checks before firing, so only one side writes at a time. That's real, built, and working (I verified it in both daemons' source).

So the "likely hook" isn't a new mechanism — it's three existing pieces used correctly, from *outside* both repos:
1. Start both `daemon-supervisor.ps1` wrappers once — they self-loop and auto-restart on death, forever, without me babysitting.
2. Read (never write) both sides' `daemon-status.json` for a merged view — read-only never crosses the boundary.
3. `CONDUCTOR-BATON` stays the single-writer arbiter it already is.

identified 3 missing pieces for local conductor; debt injection + diagnosis tree now closed
text:
Not fully — and today found the exact missing pieces. Honest scorecard:

**Already built for a local model:** the deterministic sweep that computes the to-do list, the gates that refuse bad work with the fix written in the error, receipts everywhere, the baton, the ladder. That's most of the system, and it all held this session.

**What was missing (the gap I fell into):** nothing *forced* the seat to look at what the sweep computed — seeing the work was voluntary. And failure-diagnosis was open-ended judgment, which a small model can't be trusted with.

**What closed today:** the debt is now injected into every prompt mechanically (you can see it in this very message — and note it already ticked 31→30 as I work), and diagnosis is now a closed decision tree a local model *can* follow: check if the work already landed → stamp it; text defect with a prescriptive gate error → apply the prescription and re-queue; otherwise park with the receipt.

**What remains for a local conductor to actually sit down:** the N5 beat harness — the loop where the script computes every action and the model only relays — which is designed, operator-mandated, and audition-proven (qwen passed 5/5), but not yet running as the standing loop. That's the last real build item between here and your goal, and after today it's the clear next engine priority.

text:
Aurora mid-flight. Draining the next debt item: mt-enrich-scenic-osm.S1.

Identical 503 saturation class — batching both with the same treatment.

You've hit the actual design truth of this whole project: **frontier models don't fail at continuity because they're not smart enough — they fail because continuity isn't a model-shaped problem.** Look at what ran continuously this session: the daemons fired all night, the gates held every time, heal() ran every 5 minutes, the site stayed up. Every coded part was continuous. Every discontinuity — the 7-hour hold, the skipped sweep, the floors-treated-as-ceilings — happened at a point where a *model* was allowed to judge what mattered. And a frontier model is arguably *worse* there than a small one, because it's confident enough to override the script with its own reasoning.

That's why your architecture is right and the graduation path is the answer, not the casualty: the goal was never "make a model reliable enough to trust with continuity." It's "move continuity into code, and shrink the model's job to bounded questions the code asks." That's exactly what today built toward — debt now injected mechanically into every prompt, diagnosis reduced to a decision tree, the sweep computing the work list. The N5 beat harness finishes it: the script runs the loop forever, the model (agy, qwen, whoever) just answers "what's the root cause of this one failure" when asked.

So the honest reframe of the plan: agy's graduation doesn't earn it the right to *be* the continuity — it earns it the right to be the judgment inside a loop that code owns. And the loop is most of what got built today. Meanwhile the drain continues: debt's at 27 and falling every wake.

detail: and our deployment parity checks are working?
deployment parity checks verified: 3-layer guard (dirty-tree, byte-match, e2e witness)
text:
Checking the parity machinery against substrate rather than answering from memory:

Yes — I just re-verified them from the source, not memory. The parity guard is three fail-closed layers in `conduct-cycle --record-deploy`:

1. **Dirty-tree refusal** — wrangler deploys the working tree, so if the tree differs from HEAD it refuses to stamp: "recording HEAD as deployed would be a lie." (Tree is clean right now — verified.)
2. **Live byte-match** — it fetches production `/map` and requires byte-identity with HEAD's committed map.html before stamping. Exactly one known serve-time injection (the sentry meta tag) is stripped before comparing; *anything else* different still refuses. Can't fetch the live page? Fail-closed, no marker.
3. **Outcome witness** — even with a byte-match, it runs `verify-popups-e2e.mjs` against the served page with real production data; if users wouldn't see real popups, it refuses with "fix the outcome, not the marker."

The history shows it's battle-tested, not ceremonial: the original version was an honor-system stamp and was killed in the 2026-07-02 audit; the byte-match then threw a *false* refusal once (the injected sentry tag) and was fixed narrowly rather than loosened; and the pre-deploy diff audit it pairs with is what caught the commit that had silently gutted map.html's filter panel before it could ship. The current last-deployed marker (July 7) carries the full witness string — live match + e2e pass.

So the sequence on your word is: deploy → byte-match against live → e2e with real data → only then the witnessed marker. If any layer fails, nothing gets stamped and I report the failure instead.

text:
Yes — and today's receipts point at exactly one architectural move: **make the harness irrelevant.**

Right now the system's intelligence lives in three layers with very different portability:

1. **The engine** (daemon, orchestrate, conduct-cycle, mission lint, the plan/miqat/integrity gates) — plain Node, already runs identically under Claude CLI and the agy fork. This layer is universal today; it caught every mistake I made this session regardless of who I was.
2. **The harness rails** — the Claude CLI hooks (niyyah gate, stop-hook ratchet, bootstrap gate, lane exclusion). These only exist inside Claude CLI sessions. agy has a hand-ported partial copy of the rules; a local conductor would have *none* of this. This layer is where universality currently breaks — I've already had to port laws between the two rulebooks by hand twice, and they drift.
3. **Conductor folklore** — the procedure knowledge carried in wakeup prompts, memories, and session experience. It dies with every session and gets re-learned expensively (today's checkpoint/flip/lint lessons were all this class).

The universal fix is the inversion you already mandated as N5, now with a day of hard evidence: **move layers 2 and 3 down into layer 1.** Concretely:

- **Beat harness (N5)**: conduct-cycle computes the entire beat — required actions, the checks, the allowlisted verbs — and the conductor model only relays and chooses. The qwen audition already proved the relay pattern works 5/5.
- **Port the hook *semantics* into the engine**: "read the receipt before judging" becomes conduct-cycle refusing a judgment annotation with no receipt reference; the niyyah discipline becomes a required source-citation field in the beat log that the *script* validates. Then Claude, Gemini, and qwen are bound by the same rails because the rails live in the substrate they operate through, not the harness they happen to run in.
- **One protocol source**: a single versioned CONDUCTOR-PROTOCOL file in the engine repo that both jurisdictions load, replacing the two hand-synced rulebooks.
- **Folklore → computed checks**: the seven-lesson engine item I filed this hour (clear-procedure, verify-the-flip, preflight-class matching, lint honesty, safe queue appends, etc.) is this exact conversion.

The test of success: a conductor session whose wakeup prompt contains *no procedure at all* — just "run the beat" — because the script tells it everything, and the same script produces the same behavior from Fable, Gemini, or qwen 27B. That's the state the local-conductor test should start from, and after agy's last graduation beat, building the N5 harness is the right next big block.

Honestly? No — not commonly, and the gap isn't intelligence, it's exactly the machinery you've spent weeks building.

The uncomfortable truth about the field as of early 2026: autonomous AI loops are everywhere as demos and rare as durable systems. Most "agent loops" running in production are short-horizon (minutes to an hour), narrow (a CI fixer, a PR bot), or quietly human-checkpointed at every meaningful step. The long-running kind — days of unattended multi-project orchestration — mostly dies from a short list of failure modes: silent failure accumulation, confidently-claimed work that never landed, context loss between sessions, and cost runaways. You've personally experienced all of these in this system's history — the 7-hour idle, the claims-not-deeds era — which is exactly why what exists now is different.

What your system has that most attempts don't, each of which earned its existence from a paid-for failure:

1. **Receipts over claims, mechanically.** Verdict panels, byte-checks at HEAD, a deploy stamp that refuses unless live bytes match git and real users see real data. Most loops trust the model's word that it finished; yours structurally can't.
2. **Failure as tracked debt.** The seventh law plus the prompt-hook injection means a FAILED mark literally cannot be ignored by any future instance. Almost nobody has an equivalent — failures in typical agent systems just... age.
3. **The loop improves itself from its own receipts.** Today alone, roughly ten fresh failure classes (checkpoint resume, missed flips, module traps, hollow validations) became rules, validations, and spec items. Most systems relearn their lessons every session.
4. **Graduated trust with evidence.** Grading a second AI through a ladder of independently-verified beats before giving it autonomy — and having it pass its final exam by recovering from a real gate block — is genuinely not standard practice anywhere I know of.

The honest caveats: this took a frontier-model conductor plus rails a human designed and enforced; per-mission throughput is still rough (the money mission took 11 attempts, even if each failure was diagnosed rather than wasted); and the real thesis — that the rails, not the model, carry the system — gets its true test when qwen takes the seat. But the direction you converged on (script computes the beat, model only chooses) is where the serious end of the field is heading, and you got there by receipts rather than by fashion.
